Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAP Indigenous Australians Australia’s Indigenous population estimated at 2.2m before ‘demographic catastrophe’ of colonisation Study finds earlier numbers were underestimated, suggesting impact of diseases and massacres were much greater than previously thought Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Tory Shepherd Tue 15 Sep 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 06.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The number of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia before colonisation was dramatically underestimated, according to new research that suggests many more of them were killed. Modelling by a national research group puts the population levels before the 1788 first fleet arrived at 2.2 million, compared with early estimates of 250,000 people. Stolen Generations survivors have more health challenges than other First Nations people Read more The research, by the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Indigenous and Environmental Histories and Futures (CIEHF), has been published in the peer-reviewed Nature Human Behaviour . The authors wrote that, historically, population estimates have been poor “due to lethal diseases, frontier and structural violence, and absence of systematic censuses” and that it’s “invaluable to truth-telling and reconciliation” to try to rectify that. They warn readers that the content of the study is confronting and possibly distressing. The modelling showed there had to be millions of excess deaths from smallpox and other diseases, massacres, and the other results of colonisation such as dispossession and malnutrition, according to co-author Prof Corey Bradshaw, a global ecology professor at Flinders University. His previous research found that an 1789 smallpox outbreak alone killed as many as 220,000 Aboriginal people. There were also other smallpox epidemics, as well as outbreaks of measles, influenza, tuberculosis, typhoid and other diseases. Bradshaw said he would bet his career that massacre databases were underestimated by an “order of magnitude”. “If you’re a frontier farmer, a colonialist that came out to a new area, and you were trying to remove people from ‘your’ land, you’re not going to write extensively about how many people you killed to do that,” he said. “There’s another component here that’s essentially greed and racism – the entire concept of terra nullius was based on not many people being here. If there’s a systematic desire to take land [fewer people means a] better justification for imperialism.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Australia was colonised on the basis of terra nullius , that it belonged to no one. That concept was overthrown with the high court’s Mabo decision , when it was recognised that First Nations people had been here for tens of thousands of years. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were not properly counted in the census until 1971, after the 1967 referendum . At that point, 115,953 people identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander. In 2021, 812,728 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were counted in the census, a figure revised upwards to 983,257 with post-census recounts . The estimate of 2.2 million, as well as a new estimate of 2.06 million excess deaths between 1788 and 1861, means the population was reduced to about 7% of its original size. “We are not talking about a marginal consequence of colonisation but a demographic catastrophe at the heart of the Australian story,” distinguished professor Larissa Behrendt said. A Euahleyai/Gamillaroi woman, she is also the chair of the CIEHF’s advisory committee. Early on after colonisation, various people estimated how many Aboriginal people were in their region. For example, governor Arthur Phillip estimated Gadigal people of the Eora nation came to about 1,500. The first continent-wide estimate by social anthropologist Alfred Radcliffe-Brown put the number between 250,000 and 300,000, but mainly used observations from after the impacts of colonisation had been felt. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Radcliffe-Brown was aware that it was an underestimate, but many researchers since have relied on that count as a baseline. Again, they often recognised it would be an undercount because of historical reasons and changes in who identified or was identified as Aboriginal. In 1983, economic historian Noel Butlin estimated the population at about 900,000. Later he increased that to between 1.1 million and 1.3 million. In 1987, archaeologists John Mulvaney and J Peter White argued it was more likely 750,000. Table showing estimated Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population numbers from various studies There have been many and varied estimates since, usually based on historical and ethnographic information. The Australian team used different approaches to model the population. They looked at archaeological items to reconstruct how many people would have been there at a particular time, reconstructed the climate and the productivity of the land to infer how many people it could sustain and looked at genetic data to work back in time based on known DNA mutation rates. They also reviewed, but did not rely on, ethnographic estimates. “The findings highlight the scale of demographic catastrophe experienced by Indigenous Australians due to colonisation, with the implications being a heightened understanding of intergenerational trauma and to inform future policy that assists Indigenous people,” said co-author and distinguished professor Lynette Russell of the Monash University Indigenous Studies Centre and CIEHF. The authors wrote that Australia must prioritise reconciliation, engagement and policymaking with Indigenous people who still suffer intergenerational trauma and that the broader community should embrace the rich culture that survived these events. The lead author, James Cook University associate professor Alan Williams, said the “devastating findings” highlighted the impacts of invasion. However, they also demonstrated the “remarkable survival, resilience and recovery over the past century of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island people”. Behrendt said the research “tells us something extraordinary”. “Our survival is one of Australian history’s most remarkable stories,” she said. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/11/four.text: At least four people have reportedly died since Isaias made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane on Friday, authorities have said, as forecasters warn of flooding and tornado risks as the storm pushes further inland.Isaias, which has since weakened into a post-tropical cyclone, first hit the city of Destin on Friday evening, bringing 105 mph (around 169 kph) winds as it struck the Florida Panhandle.Officials have so far reported four deaths related to the storm, including two in Florida's Escambia County and two in Alabama, according to US media reports.The US' National Hurricane Center said in an update on Saturday night that heavy rainfall was likely to continue across the southeastern US overnight and warned of possible flash and urban flooding risks as well as high winds."Swells from Isaias will continue to affect much of the Gulf coasts of the United States, Mexico, and western Cuba this weekend," it said, adding: "These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions."The Center warned that tornadoes were also possible across eastern Georgia and the Carolinas.Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said on Saturday that more than 430,000 customers remained without power in the state as the storm continued.Tracking website PowerOutage.com shows that figure has dropped to around 323,000 as of early Sunday morning. More than 80,000 people are also experiencing outages in Alabama, over 11,000 in Georgia, and roughly 11,000 in North Carolina, per the site.DeSantis said the main problem in Florida had been from high winds causing trees to fall, damaging buildings and scattering debris.Video footage circulating on social media shows torrential rain in the state and extensive damage to buildings, with some having had their roofs ripped off.

( Getty Images: Robert Prange ) abc.net.au/news/aussie-duo-and-new-world-number-one-fall-at-china-open/107226486 Link copied Share Share article Australian women's involvement at the China Open is down to just one singles player after Kimberly Birrell and Storm Hunter were both second-round casualties. World number 41 Birrell suffered a 6-4, 6-4 loss to Czech Marie Bouzkova at the WTA 1000 event in Beijing on Saturday night. Birrell, 28, who won the Korea Open last Sunday with a win over compatriot Maya Joint in the final, raced out to a 3-1 first-set lead before dropping serve twice to lose it in 42 minutes. Down 3-0 in the second, Birrell lifted and won the next four games but was broken twice more to see her involvement in the Chinese capital come to a premature end. For Bouzkova, the 28-year-old 18th seed, a meeting with China's Zheng Qinwen awaits. The 2024 Olympic champion was leading Anna Kalinskaya 6-7 (4/7), 6-4, 3-0 when the Russian retired. Earlier, Queensland veteran and former doubles world number one Storm Hunter was beaten 6-2, 6-2 by Maria Sakkari in just 73 minutes. The 182nd-ranked Hunter failed to join 20-year-old fellow Aussie Taylah Preston in round three, losing serve six times in her latest hardcourt tournament clash in Asia. Next up for Sakkari, the Greek 25th seed and former world number three, is Elina Svitolina. The sixth-seeded Ukrainian came from a set down to eliminate Czech Katerina Siniakova, 1-6, 6-4, 6-2. Loading Twitter content Shock of the day came with newly crowned world number one Elena Rybakina crashing out ‌3-6, 6-4, 6-3 to unseeded Alina Charaeva in the second round. It couldn't have been a worse start to her reign as the number one as Rybakina lost in her first match since defeating four-times major winner Aryna Sabalenka to capture the US Open title last month. Charaeva, a 24-year-old Russian-born Armenian ranked 118th ​in the world, etched her name into the record books by becoming the lowest-ranked competitor since the introduction of the WTA rankings in 1975 to rally from a set down to defeat a world number one. Elsewhere, there were wins for third seed Coco Gauff, eighth seed Iga Swiatek, 21st seed Ann Li and 24th seed Jelena Ostapenko.
